title: Genuina principia doctrinae de statu aequilibrii et motu corporum tam perfecte flesibilium quam elasticorum

deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is Euler's planar theory of rods. A thread with arc length s has tangent angle Φ, so its curvature is k = dΦ/ds. At each point there is a tangential force T (tension) and a normal (shear) force V. Their moment Vv, where v is a lever arm, is the bending moment. The thread carries distributed tangential and normal loads p and q per unit length.

The three general balance equations from the previous section, in modern form, are:
- (I) T' + V k = p
- (II) V' − T k = q
- (III) (Vv)' = V, i.e. moment balance with M = Vv.

Case 2 (uniformly elastic, naturally straight thread). The constitutive law from the previous page is M = Vv = A k, with A constant (bending stiffness).

Derivation on the page:
1. Law (III) gives A k' = V. With ds constant this is V = A ddΦ/ds².
2. The lever arm follows as v = M/V = ds dΦ/ddΦ.
3. Substituting into (I) gives T' = p − A k k'. Integrating, T = ∫p ds − A k²/2.
4. Equation (II) gives T = (A k'' − q)/k, printed as A d³Φ/(dΦ ds²) − q ds/dΦ.
5. Equating the two expressions for T and multiplying by 2k gives the curve equation 2A k'' + A k³ = 2k∫p ds + 2q. In modern form: A(k'' + k³/2) = k∫p ds + q.

Euler remarks that since dΦ already contains second differentials of the coordinates, the equation is of fourth order in Cartesian terms.

With p = q = 0 this is the intrinsic equation of the free elastica, k'' + k³/2 − λk = 0, with λ = T0/A. This is the stationary mKdV / elastica equation.

The page then announces the generalization to non-uniform threads (stiffness S(s)) and to threads that are naturally curved. These are treated on the following pages.
errors: The second displayed value is labelled 'V' (V = A d³Φ/(dΦ ds²) − q ds/dΦ), but it is the expression for T obtained from equation II, T = (dV − q ds)/dΦ. This is a slip in the original printing; the final equation is correct only if it is read as T.
The constant of integration in T = ∫p ds − A dΦ²/(2ds²) is absorbed into the indefinite integral ∫p ds. This is not an error, but it is implicit.

ideas.what: Balance of forces and moments for a planar rod, with tension T and shear force V as separate unknowns, plus a constitutive moment law M = A·curvature
ideas.modern_name: Kirchhoff–Clebsch style planar rod equations (force and moment balance, Euler–Bernoulli moment law)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E410, 1771); emphasized by Truesdell (1960) as the first correct general rod theory with shear force
ideas.where_published: E410, Novi Comm. Acad. Sci. Petrop. 15 (1771); Opera omnia II.11; analysed in Truesdell, Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies 1638–1788

ideas.what: Intrinsic curvature equation of the loaded elastica: A(k'' + k³/2) = k∫p ds + q
ideas.modern_name: Intrinsic (curvature–arclength) elastica equation; stationary mKdV for p = q = 0
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (elastica 1744 via variational methods; intrinsic form with loads here); the mKdV connection to Goldstein–Petrich and Langer–Singer (c.1984–1991)
ideas.where_published: E410; related results in E65 Additamentum I (1744)

ideas.what: Tension in a free elastica equals the axial load minus A k²/2
ideas.modern_name: First integral of the rod equations / conserved quantity of the elastica
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler; standard in Love's Treatise on elasticity

deep.surprise_reason: The page derives the classical intrinsic elastica equation with distributed loads. This is well documented and credited to Euler via Truesdell's detailed study of E410. The only notable detail is the printing slip of V for T. The link to the mKdV equation is already in the modern literature.
transcription_corrections: 'dVv = V ds' should be read as d(Vv) = V ds (the differential of the moment Vv).
'A d · dΦ/ds = V ds' means A·d(dΦ/ds) = V ds.
The second boxed formula is printed as 'V = A d³Φ/(dΦ ds²) − q ds/dΦ' in the original. The transcription is faithful, but the left-hand side should mathematically be T.
